samples.summary: A peer-writable "poison pill" now permanently blocks copy/import/replace of a shared document (persistent DoS)
samples.evidence:
The change converts a previously-tolerated shape into a hard, irreversible refusal, and the shape is reachable by anyone who can write the Yorkie doc. Nothing server-side validates direct Yorkie tree writes (the only content validator is `PUT /content` in docs-content.controller.ts), so a collaborator using a raw SDK client — or simply an older tab/build without this cap, which had no cap at all — can write rows under a table nested at depth >= MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH, exactly as the new test fixture `peerRowsPastTheCap()` does (packages/frontend/tests/app/docs/yorkie-doc-store.test.ts) with `root.content.editByPath(...)`. Once that state exists:

1. backend: `documentHasTableAtNestingCap(content)` at document-copy.service.ts:446 throws BadRequestException on every copy, forever — the document can never be duplicated, promoted to another workspace, or used as a template. `readDocsRoot` returns the truncated model, so the condition is permanently true and there is no repair path on the server.
2. frontend: `writeFullDocument` (yorkie-doc-store.ts:3524) throws, so `setDocument` — the import-apply path (apply-imported-content.ts:226, docs-view.tsx:396) — fails for that document.
3. frontend: `updateBlock` (~1881), `updateTableCell` (~3096), `setHeader`/`setFooter` silently `return` after a `console.warn`, so edits that replace the enclosing block/cell are dropped with no user-visible signal.

The attacker capability required is only "write access to the document", which in a collaborative editor is every invited collaborator; the effect is permanent and affects all other users of that document. The design doc (docs/design/docs/tables/docs-nested-tables.md) acknowledges the wedge ("permanently blocking every replacing write over the block that holds them") but ships no repair/override path and no user-facing error.

samples.summary: `replacesTruncatedRows` guard fails open (or throws) when the tree path does not resolve
samples.evidence: `replacesTruncatedRows` returns `false` — i.e. "safe to overwrite" — whenever the tree is missing (`if (!tree || typeof tree.getRootTreeNode !== 'function') return false;`), and `getTreeBlockNode` (line 1271) returns `undefined` for an index that exists in the cached model but not in the tree, which `treeHasTruncatedRows` also answers `false` for. The guard's whole purpose is to stop a write that would delete rows the reader never read, so any cache/tree divergence (a concurrent remote edit landing between `getDocument()` and the write) silently reverts to the destructive behaviour the guard was added to prevent. Worse, `getTreeBlockNode` does `((node as ElementNode).children ?? [])[idx]` without guarding `node` itself, so an *intermediate* missing node throws a TypeError from the middle of an editor command (`updateBlock`/`updateTableCell`) rather than declining. A guard against replicated data loss should fail closed (decline) on an unresolvable path, not open.

samples.summary: Revision-snapshot recursion bound counts only `row` nodes, so non-row nesting in an attacker-supplied snapshot is still unbounded
samples.evidence: `normalizeYsonTreeNode` increments `depth` only when `node.type === 'row'` and only skips children for a `row` past the cap; every other node type recurses with the same depth and no bound. A snapshot whose tree nests e.g. `block > block > block ...` (or `cell > cell > ...`, or any unknown type — the YSON node `type` is just a string off the wire) recurses once per node with nothing to stop it, so the new cap does not actually bound this walk for shapes other than well-formed tables. The only thing standing between that and a stack overflow in the history preview is `YSON.parse`'s own incidental recursion limit, which the function's own comment concedes is "one SDK release away from changing". An absolute node-depth counter (independent of node type) would make the bound real.

samples.summary: The `Math.max(...rows)` RangeError pattern this change folded in two places remains in the markdown serializer and clipboard table parsers
samples.evidence: The diff explicitly folds `Math.max(...)` over row arrays in packages/docs/src/model/range-slices.ts:57 and packages/docs/src/view/selection.ts:214 because "`Math.max(...rows)` throws `RangeError` past ~100k arguments, and the row count is a peer's to choose — rows carry no numeric band because they are structure, not an attribute". The identical pattern over the same peer-chosen row/cell counts survives at packages/docs/src/serialize/markdown.ts:180 (`Math.max(...rows.map((r) => r.length))`, rows taken straight from a CRDT `tableData`, reached by copy-as-markdown and the CLI export) and at packages/docs/src/view/clipboard.ts:323, :891, :971, :1055 (rows from an untrusted clipboard payload / pasted HTML from a hostile page). A peer writing a table with >~125k rows, or a crafted clipboard payload, turns those into an uncaught RangeError. Searched: ripgrep for `Math\.(max|min)\(\s*(0,\s*)?\.\.\.` across packages/ excluding tests; read each docs/ hit for provenance of the spread array.
searchedFor: read packages/docs/src/model/range-slices.ts and view/selection.ts fold sites

samples.summary: `PUT /content` now rejects one nesting level that its own `GET` emits and its writer accepts
samples.evidence: `assertValidBlock` throws for *any* block at `depth >= MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH`, but the readers/writers allow tables at depths 0..31, which means ordinary (non-table) blocks legitimately live at depth 32: `treeNodeToBlock` reads a table at depth 31 and hands its cell blocks depth 32, and `documentHasTableAtNestingCap` only refuses a *table* at >= 32. So `GET /content` on a document at the maximum legal nesting returns a body that its own `PUT` answers with 400 `blocks are nested too deeply`, and the newly capped DOCX importer (which keeps tables at depths 0..31, per the new test asserting `importedDepth === MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH`) produces exactly such a body for the CLI's `docs import`. The fail direction is the safe one, but it denies a legitimate round-trip; the check should be on the table block (`b.type === 'table' && depth >= cap`) to match the writer's invariant.

verdict.reason: The cited code exists (document-copy.service.ts:446 throws on documentHasTableAtNestingCap; docs-tree.ts:231-256 defines the predicate; yorkie-doc-store.ts:3524-3531 throws; the test fixture at yorkie-doc-store.test.ts:3784-3822 really does craft the shape with a raw editByPath). It is nonetheless not a blocking issue under the Security lens. (a) No privilege boundary is crossed: the required capability is document write access, and such a principal can already destroy the document's content via ordinary CRDT ops; the refusal grants no new authority, no data exposure, and is not authz/secrets/injection/crypto/SSRF/deserialization/path-traversal. The "silent return with console.warn, no user-visible signal" half is squarely the correctness/design lens. (b) The finding's load-bearing premise — "permanently blocks ... no repair path on the server" — is false in this repo: PUT /api/v1/workspaces/:workspaceId/documents/:documentId/content (docs-content.controller.ts:164-218) never reads existing state; it validates only the incoming body (line 191) and calls writeDocsRoot(root, body) (line 214), whose cap check inspects only the incoming document (docs-tree.ts:376) before wiping all existing children (docs-tree.ts:394-398). Any caller passing CombinedAuthGuard/WorkspaceScopeGuard/ApiKeyWriteScopeGuard (docs-content.controller.ts:100) with a shallow body clears the deep chain, so the wedge is recoverable through a guarded, documented API rather than permanent. What remains is a recoverable availability/UX degradation inducible only by an already-authorized writer — out of this lens's lane and not merge-blocking under its rubric.
